title: Open Problem (characterizing edge probabilities for Theorem 1.1)
statement_text: Characterize all edge probabilities $p = p(n)$ for which the following holds whp for the random graph $G=G(n,p)$: $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})=\left(1-\frac{1}{k-1}+o(1)\right)p\binom{n}{2}$, where $\mathcal{P}$ is a non-trivial hereditary property and $k=k(\mathcal{P})$ is the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in $\mathcal{P}$.
context_text: A graph property $\mathcal{P}$ is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs (and isomorphism); it is non-trivial if it contains all edgeless graphs and misses some graph. For a graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})$ is the maximum number of edges of a subgraph of $G$ (not necessarily induced) that belongs to $\mathcal{P}$. $k=k(\mathcal{P})\ge2$ is the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in $\mathcal{P}$, $G(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and whp means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. The authors prove that for every fixed $p\in(0,1)$, whp $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P})=(1-\frac{1}{k-1}+o(1))p\binom n2$, and that the same holds whenever $n^{-c}\le p\le1-n^{-c}$ for a constant $c=c(\mathcal{P})>0$. For principal monotone properties (avoiding a single graph as a subgraph) the exact range of $p$ is known (Conlon–Gowers, Schacht), but hereditary properties are far more general (e.g. perfect graphs, or graphs with no induced copy of a given graph). The authors note that it is not difficult to find hereditary (even monotone) properties for which the fraction of edges of $G(n,p)$ lying in a maximum subgraph with the property changes, whp, several times as $p=p(n)$ increases from 0 to 1; presumably the answer depends on $\mathcal{P}$.

title: Open Problem (accurate estimate in the bipartite case)
statement_text: Provide a more accurate estimate for $\mathrm{ex}(G, \mathcal{P})$, $G=G(n,p)$, when the non-trivial hereditary property $\mathcal{P}$ misses a bipartite graph (i.e., when $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P}) = o(n^2)$ whp).
context_text: A graph property $\mathcal{P}$ is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs (and isomorphism); it is non-trivial if it contains all edgeless graphs and misses some graph. For a graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})$ is the maximum number of edges of a subgraph of $G$ (not necessarily induced) that belongs to $\mathcal{P}$. $k=k(\mathcal{P})\ge2$ is the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in $\mathcal{P}$, $G(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and whp means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. The authors prove that for every fixed $p\in(0,1)$, whp $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P})=(1-\frac{1}{k-1}+o(1))p\binom n2$, and that the same holds whenever $n^{-c}\le p\le1-n^{-c}$ for a constant $c=c(\mathcal{P})>0$. For principal monotone properties (avoiding a single graph as a subgraph) the exact range of $p$ is known (Conlon–Gowers, Schacht), but hereditary properties are far more general (e.g. perfect graphs, or graphs with no induced copy of a given graph). When $\mathcal{P}$ misses a bipartite graph, $k(\mathcal{P})=2$ and the theorem only gives $\mathrm{ex}(G(n,p),\mathcal{P})=o(n^2)$ whp, without the precise order of magnitude. The authors suggest that it is plausible that $\mathrm{ex}(G,\mathcal{P})\le n^{2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(\mathcal{P})>0$ in this case.

title: Informal Conjecture (polynomial saving in the bipartite case)
statement_text: It seems plausible that in the bipartite case (the non-trivial hereditary property $\mathcal{P}$ misses some bipartite graph) one has, for $G=G(n,p)$ whp, $\mathrm{ex}(G, \mathcal{P}) \leq n^{2-\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\mathcal{P}) > 0$.
